title: Integrations pages that tell the truth
excerpt: List the connections a customer can turn on this week, what each one does, and what it does not do. A logo for a tool you might support later is a promise you will have to take back.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, connections that exist drawn as lines rather than a wall of logos.
caption: String between printed screens. An integration is a connection that does a job. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an integrations page list?
faqs.answer: Only connections a customer could turn on this week. For each one, write the name, the job that moves and in which direction, and the limit. A conversation, a prototype, or a logo you hope to support later does not belong on the page.

faqs.question: How should you handle tools customers ask for that you do not support?
faqs.answer: Give them one request line at the bottom, and keep the list private. Do not publish greyed-out logos. A repeated job in that private list is a candidate to build. A repeated logo with no job is not.

faqs.question: What should the page say when a connection breaks?
faqs.answer: Say so in the same week, on the page or in the product, and say what the customer can do in the meantime. Leaving a tile looking healthy while the export is delayed is a fiction. A status without a next step is only an apology.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An integrations page lists what actually connects, what the connection does, and what it does not do. A saas integrations page made of logos you might support later is a promise. You will walk it back on a sales call, or in a support thread, after a buyer has already planned their week around it.

Publish the connections you can demo. Label anything else as a request, not as a tile. The difference is the whole page.

## The three lines each connection needs

The name, written in text, with the mark if you have the right to use it. The name matters more than the mark. A buyer searching for their tool should find the word.

The job. What moves, and in which direction. Orders flow into the warehouse tool. Invoices export as a file. Users can sign in with the identity provider. "We integrate with X" is not a job. It is a shrug. Write the object and the verb.

The limit. What does not sync. What requires a plan. What the customer must already have on the other side. A one-way export is not a two-way sync. A nightly file is not a live connection. The limit is how you stay trustworthy when the buyer's colleague asks a sharper question than the logo invited.

Add a fourth line only when it changes the decision: who sets it up, and roughly what they need. An admin, a key, a warehouse ID. You do not need a full setup novel on this page. Link to the guide. If the guide does not exist, the connection is not ready to be public, or the line should say "we set this up with you" if that is the truth.

Order the lines the same way every time. Name, job, limit. A buyer learning the pattern on the first entry can scan the rest. A page that gives one partner a case study and the next a logo is a partner page that lost the plot. This page is a catalog of jobs.

## What "actually connects" means

It means a customer could turn it on this week and the job would happen. A prototype in a branch does not count. A partnership conversation does not count. A Zapier account someone on your team once made does not count, unless you support that path and will help when it breaks.

It means you know who owns the failure. When the other side changes an API, someone on your team notices, or the page changes. A tile with no owner is how a dead integration stays on the marketing site for a year.

It means the words match the product. If the button in the product says "Export CSV" and the page says "native sync," you have written a different product. Use the product's verb. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public examples of product interfaces that have to be scannable. An integrations page is the same kind of object. A person should be able to scan a row and leave with a yes or a no.

If the connection exists only for one legacy customer, leave it off the public page or mark it as limited. A logo implies a door. A door that is really a favor will be tried by the next buyer, who will not get the favor, and will remember.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks you to avoid claims a reader cannot trust, and to show first-hand experience. The experience here is dull and perfect: you have set the connection up, you know the limit, and you can say it. A logo grid of aspirations shows the opposite. It shows a list of markets you wish you were in.

## How to group them

Group by the job the buyer has. Sign-in. Payments. Shipping. Accounting. Data in. Data out. Identity. If you only have three connections, you may not need groups. A short list with the three lines is enough. Groups are for when the list becomes a wall.

Inside a group, put the connection most customers use first. The rare enterprise option can sit lower with its limit in the open. Fame is a weak sort. The buyer's stack is the sort that matters. If you know you win when a company already uses a particular ledger, that ledger can lead the accounting group. Say why in the line, not in a footnote.

Offer search once the list is long enough that scanning fails. Search should match the customer's word, including the common misspelling and the old product name after an acquisition. If you cannot maintain those aliases, skip search and keep the groups tight.

Do not group by "coming soon." That group is a promise board. If you want demand, use a single line at the bottom: tell us what you need. That is a request, and it does not wear a logo. You can learn from it. You should not let it look like a catalog.

A partner page and this page are cousins. The partner page says what the relationship does for the customer. The integrations page says what the software connection does. If a relationship has no connection, it does not belong here. It belongs on the partner page, with a sentence, or it belongs nowhere public.

## Setup, status, and the truth when it breaks

Link each connection to the shortest setup that works. If setup is a call, say that, and say what the customer should prepare. If setup is a switch in the product, show the switch. A product led page can carry the picture. This catalog can carry a crop and a link.

Say whether you charge. Included in every plan, included in one plan, or quoted. A pricing shape belongs on the pricing page. Here, one phrase is enough, and it must match. A contradiction between the integrations page and the pricing page is the kind of thing a champion gets blamed for internally. Do not do that to them.

When a connection is degraded, say so on the page or in the product, in the same week. "Export is delayed" is a status. Leaving the tile glowing green is a fiction. You can keep the tile and add the status. Removing it without a word is how a customer thinks they imagined the feature.

Write what the customer can do in the meantime. Download the file. Use the older path. Wait. A status without a next step is an apology. A next step is a product.

Keep a private list of connections you refused. The reasons are useful the next time a logo request arrives. "We will not imply a sync we do not have." That sentence, agreed once, saves every future argument in the marketing meeting.

## A request path that is not a tile

People will ask for tools you do not connect to. Give them one place to ask, at the bottom of the page, in a sentence. "Tell us the tool and the job you need done." Store the answers. Read them monthly. A repeated job is a candidate for a real connection. A repeated logo with no job is not. Build the job, then add the tile with its three lines.

Do not turn those requests into public cards that look like the real catalog. A greyed logo is still a logo. Procurement will screenshot it. You will then explain, in a questionnaire, that the screenshot was a wish. That explanation costs more than the discipline of leaving the logo off.

When you do ship a new connection, update the page the same day the switch exists in the product. A blog post is not the catalog. The catalog is the page a buyer checks at 11 p.m. without you in the room. If the page is late, the buyer will test the product, fail, and decide you were careless. The release note can celebrate. The integrations page has to be true first.

Keep the request list private, with the reason you said no, so the next person on your team does not relitigate it from scratch. "No two-way payment sync. We export a file." That note is an asset. A public mural of maybes is a liability. The page stays short because the private list is allowed to be long.

## The sales conversation this page is for

A good page makes the call shorter. The buyer has already seen that you export invoices and do not post payments back. The call can start at their edge case. A bad page makes the call a correction. The buyer arrives believing you are in their stack, and you spend the first ten minutes taking logos away. Nielsen Norman Group's observation about the first 10 seconds is relevant even here. The value of this page is a fast no, or a fast yes, not a mood of compatibility.

Coach the team to send the specific anchor, not the whole grid. A link to the accounting section beats a link to the top of a mural. The heading of that section should be real, so the URL or the jump lands on words that match the email.

When a buyer asks for something you do not have, the page gives you a sentence. "We do not connect to that yet. Here is the request path." That is easier to say when the page never showed the logo. It is miserable to say when the logo has been on the site since last spring.

Update the talk track when you add a limit. The person who writes the page and the person who sells should read the three lines together before a launch. A Hanabi build would treat those lines as content in the site, editable without a scavenger hunt, in the same Next.js project as the rest of the marketing pages. The portal, after delivery, holds the notes so the limits are not trapped in a slide.

If customers must move off an old connection and onto a new one, the catalog is the wrong genre. They need the order of steps, what breaks, and how long it takes. The piece on [a migration guide for your own customers](/blog/a-migration-guide-for-your-own-customers) is the next read when a tile is being replaced rather than merely described.

When a connection list has turned into a mural of intentions, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the list of what works this week and the list of logos someone wants to add. The call should end with the three lines, and with a smaller page.
